title: Japan: Bank of Japan rate rises, weak yen and equity sell-off
what_happened: The Bank of Japan set its policy rate at around 1.25% in September 2026 and said it would continue to raise it. The yen traded near 159 to 160 per dollar in mid-November. A fall of about 5% in the Nikkei 225 on 2026-11-20 was widely reported but is not yet confirmed here.
how_it_reaches_markets: Higher Japanese yields can pull Japanese capital home from US and other foreign bonds; sharp yen moves can force unwinding of yen-funded positions; possible currency intervention.

sourced_facts.text: 2026-09-18: Bank of Japan set the guideline for the uncollateralized overnight call rate at around 1.25 percent, effective 2026-09-24, by a 7-2 vote; the statement says the Bank will continue to raise the policy interest rate
Yen per dollar, Federal Reserve noon rates: 159.65 on 2026-11-16, 159.76 on 2026-11-19, 158.76 on 2026-11-20 (H.10 release of 2026-11-23)

resolved_when_all: USD/JPY stays below 155 for 20 consecutive trading days without reported intervention
The Bank of Japan completes a policy meeting whose decision matches the majority forecast and the Nikkei 225 does not fall more than 3% on that day or the next
worsened_when_any: The Nikkei 225 falls more than 5% in a day again
Japan's 10-year government bond yield closes above 3.0%

relief_headlines_that_do_not_resolve_it: Single-day rebounds (the Nikkei rose 3.91% on 2026-11-24 and fell 2.78% on 2026-11-25)
Verbal warnings by officials against excessive currency moves

counter_view.note: The strongest reason this card's reading may be wrong. AFMX's own judgment, using the facts listed on the card.
counter_view.text: The Bank of Japan has moved in small steps and said in advance that it would keep raising. A weak yen also lifts exporters' earnings. Sharp spillovers from Japan to the US market have been rare, so this may remain a local story.

forecasts.basis: A Bank of Japan meeting that matches forecasts is likely; the yen staying below 155 for 20 days from about 159 is not. Any one of three things worsens the card: confirmed intervention, a 5% one-day fall in the Nikkei, or a 10-year yield above 3.0% (reported near 2.8%).
